blogs.title: From Ciminelli to Kousisis: Redefining Fraud’s Property Requirement in Securities Cases
blogs.description: This post dissects how the Fifth Circuit reconciled the Supreme Court’s rulings in *Ciminelli v. United States* and *Kousisis v. United States* to uphold an indictment for a pump‑and‑dump scheme. It explains the distinction between the rejected “right‑to‑control” theory and the affirmed “fraudulent‑inducement” theory, explores what counts as “money or property” under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1348/1349, and assesses the broader doctrinal shift away from a narrow property interest requirement in federal fraud statutes.

blogs.title: Pump‑and‑Dump in the Age of Instagram and TikTok: Prosecuting ‘Finfluencers’ Under Federal Securities Law
blogs.description: Focusing on the facts of *United States v. Constantinescu*, this article examines how social‑media influencers weaponize platforms to run classic pump‑and‑dump schemes. It evaluates whether current securities statutes are equipped to target coordinated online promotion, discusses enforcement challenges posed by algorithmic amplification and jurisdictional issues, and considers whether new FTC guidance or legislative amendments are needed to curb so‑called “Finfluencer” fraud.

blogs.title: Pleading Fraud: De Novo Review versus Rule 8(b) – Lessons from United States v. Constantinescu
blogs.description: The Fifth Circuit’s de novo analysis of indictment sufficiency offers a roadmap for criminal prosecutors. This post breaks down the court’s approach to evaluating alleged scheme‑to‑defraud and intent elements under Rule 8(b), contrasts it with heightened pleading standards in civil fraud cases, and provides practical takeaways for drafting indictments that survive early dismissal motions after *Constantinescu*.

blogs.title: Conspiracy Across Platforms: The Reach of §1349 in Multi‑Defendant Influencer Schemes
blogs.description: When dozens of influencers coordinate deceptive posts across Twitter, YouTube, and Discord, can they be charged with conspiracy under 18 U.S.C. § 1349? This article analyzes how *Constantinescu* treats conspiracy liability among socially dispersed actors, outlines evidentiary thresholds for showing a common unlawful goal, and discusses emerging doctrines—such as “joint venture” liability and digital communication footprints—that will shape future multi‑defendant fraud prosecutions.
